profile.name: Sasa
profile.tagline: A Samoan body percussion dance of seated rows striking thighs and hands in unison.
profile.insight: First noted in academic literature by Buck in 1927, sasa translates literally to strike, transforming village rows into living canoes.
profile.profile: Sasa is a folk dance from Samoa performed by all ages and genders, traditionally as a village activity. The word sāsā means "to strike," featuring precise claps, slaps, and intricate hand gestures depicting daily life. While mostly seated, performers occasionally stand during the course of the dance.
profile.profile_long: Sasa originated as a village activity in Samoa, performed by whole groups to achieve a powerful visual and auditory effect for viewers. Academic literature first mentioned a dance by this name in Buck's field notes from 1927–28, though those descriptions closely resembled a different dance, siva lapalapa. The word sasa is cognate with other Polynesian terms like Māori haka and Hawaiian ha'a. Sasa is performed by large groups of people, typically seated, though specific parts of the performance require the group to stand up. Movements include precise rhythmic claps, body slaps, and hand gestures depicting everyday activities such as cooking an umu, paddling a canoe, cleaning, or observing fish in water and birds in the sky. A leader called the fa'aluma directs the group, starting the performance by yelling "tulolo" to instruct dancers to bow their heads, and "nofo" for them to sit upright, while chanting words like "Talofa" at the beginning and "Tofa" at the end. Every sasa differs, incorporating traditional movements that have never changed alongside newly added contemporary moves. The Samoa 'ava ceremony is always included in the sasa, where the group mimics the Taupōu making 'ava.

A leader called the fa'aluma directs the group, starting with "tulolo" to bow heads and "nofo" to sit upright, while shouting chants like "Talofa" or "Tofa".

teaching.formation: Large group, normally seated in rows
teaching.level_notes: Performed by all ages and genders; movements range from traditional gestures to newly added contemporary moves.

music_profile.vocal_style: Chants like 'Talofa' at the beginning and 'Tofa' at the end, directed by the fa'aluma yelling 'tulolo' and 'nofo'.

movement_profile.posture: Usually seated, with parts of the dance requiring the group to stand up.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Precise, rhythmic claps and intricate hand movements depicting everyday practices, fish, birds, cooking, cleaning, and paddling.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Large group of people, traditionally whole villages, moving into formations like a large canoe with arms mimicking paddles.

signature_moves.name: Canoe paddling
signature_moves.description: Arms on the outside mimic the movement of paddles in the water while the group forms a large canoe.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Seated and standing levels; jumps not described in sources.

learning_units.description: Execute seated response to fa'aluma commands tulolo and nofo.

prerequisites.description: Ability to sit in rows and perform upper body percussive strikes.

feedback_rules.description: Compare timing of hand slaps to group unison; note that individual gesture variations exist as modern moves are added.

social_formats.description: Large group formation, traditionally whole villages sitting in rows.

activation_questions.question: What specific rhythm patterns or tempos are traditionally used by the fa'aluma during a sasa performance?
activation_questions.why_needed: Sources note the use of chants and striking, but lack explicit musical structure or tempo details.
activation_questions.next_evidence: Ethnomusicological field recordings or instructional manuals of Samoan dance.

episode_brief.title_hook: Striking in Unison: The Power of the Samoan Sasa
episode_brief.logline: A village of performers sits in rows, slapping thighs and clapping in synchrony to tell the story of daily life.
beats: Introduction by the fa'aluma yelling 'tulolo' to bow heads.
Sitting upright on the command 'nofo' and opening with a chant like 'Talofa'.
Executing rhythmic claps and hand gestures depicting cooking and cleaning.
Transitioning into a large canoe formation with paddling arm movements.
Standing up for designated standing sections of the dance.

lesson_ladder.goal: Learn basic seated claps and responses to fa'aluma commands.

episode_brief.instructor_persona: A knowledgeable Samoan cultural practitioner or community dance leader.
episode_brief.music_cue: Chanted vocal cues combined with body percussion slaps.

connections.name: siva lapalapa
connections.note: Early descriptions by Buck confused sasa with siva lapalapa.

seniors.seated_version: Performed from a stable chair maintaining the seated upper-body claps and gestures.
seniors.standing_version: Omit standing sections if mobility requires remaining seated.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Modify arm extension range and reduce striking force to protect joints.

children.game_version: A call-and-response rhythm game following the fa'aluma commands ('tulolo' and 'nofo').
avoid: Complex canoe spatial formations without supervision

claims.text: Sasa is a folk dance from Samoa.
claims.quote: Sasa, also spelled sāsā, is a type of folk dance from Samoa.

claims.text: It is performed by all ages and genders, usually in groups while seated.
claims.quote: Sasa is performed by all ages and genders, usually in groups and while seated.

claims.text: The word sasa means to strike and features rhythmic claps and hand movements.
claims.quote: The word "sāsā" literally means "to strike", and is characterized by precise, rhythmic claps and intricate hand movements.

claims.text: Movements depict everyday life, practices, and history like cooking, paddling, or cleaning.
claims.quote: The movements of sasa often depict Samoan practices and history, with individual gestures representing actions from everyday life, such as cooking, paddling canoes, or cleaning.

claims.text: Buck's 1927-28 field notes first mention a dance named sasa in academic literature.
claims.quote: A dance by the name of sasa is first mentioned in the academic literature in Buck's field notes from 1927–28

claims.text: Whole villages traditionally performed it for maximum effect on viewers.
claims.quote: It was traditionally performed by whole villages in order to give a perfect effect on the viewers

claims.text: Large groups perform it sitting down, with parts requiring standing.
claims.quote: Generally, the sasa is performed by a large group of people, it is normally performed sitting down, but there are parts of the dance which require the group to stand up.

claims.text: The fa'aluma begins the dance by yelling tulolo to bow heads and nofo to sit up.
claims.quote: A Sasa will always begin with the fa'aluma yelling tulolo which tells the group to bow their heads, and nofo for the group to sit up again
